newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Sugar to quit in Amstrad restructure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sugar to quit in Amstrad restructure.

text.p: British entrepreneur Alan Sugar is to take a back seat in the Amstrad Plc company he founded after the consumer electronics firm announced a restructuring on Tuesday.

The reorganisation could net Amstrad chairman Sugar about 100 million pounds ($160 million) plus a 34 percent share in Viglen Technology, the new holding company that will replace Amstrad on the London stock market in August.
The outspoken Sugar, who founded the company in 1968 and helped to popularise the home computer in Britain, will be a non-executive director of Viglen, an Amstrad spokesman said.
However, Sugar's other role as chairman and largest shareholder in London soccer club Tottenham Hotspur, will keep him in the public eye.

For each Amstrad share, shareholders will receive one Viglen Technology share plus a pro rata share of Amstrad's stake in its Betacom unit, part of the proceeds of litigation and 163 pence nominal of loan notes exchangeable for cash.
An Amstrad spokesman said the package should be worth 2.45 pounds per share plus the Viglen share. Sugar has about 40 million Amstrad shares, owning a little more than a third of the company.
The market welcomed the news, Amstrad shares adding 13p to 276.5p by 1000 GMT to value the company at around 330 million pounds.
After the restructuring, the Viglen mail order personal computer business will be the main trading arm of the company. Amstrad will remain purely as a subsidiary to pursue litigation.
Amstrad has smoothed the path for the return of value to shareholders with a number of recent moves.
It sold its Dancall Telecom mobile phone business to Germany's Robert Bosch for 92 million pounds in April. It has also sold its satellite dish business to its 70-percent owned Betacom unit.
The company was last month awarded 57 million pounds in a British legal action against Seagate Technology Inc over the purchase of hard disk drives made by Seagate.

Amstrad is seeking a total settlement of 105 million pounds, including interest on a claim dating back to 1989. It is also taking action against Western Digital Corp, again for allegedly faulty disk drives, with a hearing set for later this year in California.
Amstrad's elementary home computers gave thousands of British users their first taste of the PC in the 1970s and led to a flotation in 1980.
The company subsequently added word processing to the Amstrad computer platform and the stock roared ahead to a market valuation of one billion pounds.
But things began to turn sour as large U.S. and Japanese rivals began to erode Amstrad's share of the computer market. Relations between Sugar and Amstrad's retailers also deteriorated.

Five years ago Sugar showed his discontent with the world of shareholder finance by offering to take Amstrad back into private ownership in a deal valuing the group at just 113 million pounds. Shareholders turned him down.

Last year, Psion Plc, which manufactures hand-held personal organisers, offered to buy the company in a deal worth a minimum of 230 million pounds. But talks broke down without an agreement. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
